How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability).

Provenance, kept so that a TRACE Research Object (TRO) declaration of the run can be written later from a stored result (metacheck #404; the helpers are in R/provenance.R). Only when code was run (execute = TRUE): * run_results$started_at, run_results$ended_at: when each run of a script started and ended (ISO 8601, UTC, milliseconds); NA for a script that was not started. A script run again in a later pass has the times of its last run. A TRO uses them for each trov:TransparentResearchPerformance. * run_results$exit_status: the exit status of the process that ran the script (0 = ended normally); NA when the process did not report one (a time limit, or Docker failing to start the container). * artifacts: one row per file, with stage (deposit: as downloaded from the repository, hashed from the downloaded file; before_run: the run folder just before the first script ran, after metacheck’s own changes, such as rewritten paths and unpacked archives; after_run: only the files the scripts made (status new), changed (changed) or removed (removed), as an unchanged file is the one listed before the run), path (relative to the run folder, as valid UTF-8, a byte of another encoding written as <xx>), size (bytes), sha256, mime_type (by extension, NA when unknown), source (the file’s address in the repository, for deposit). The package libraries metacheck installs in the run folder are left out, as are metacheck’s own files there (a script’s runner, and the statistical output it writes in statistical_output/). Files metacheck itself copied or made between passes (see modifications, output_copied, file_placed) show in after_run too. A TRO uses the rows as trov:ResearchArtifacts and each stage as a trov:ArtifactArrangement. * modifications$sha256_before, modifications$sha256_after: the hash of the changed script as downloaded and as it ran; NA when the script is not at the same path in both (a script made from an R Markdown file). * environment: the system that ran the code (trov:TransparentResearchSystem in a TRO): metacheck_version, started_at, ended_at, host (R version, platform, operating system), sandbox, network_isolated (TRUE only when every Docker run had --network none; the process sandbox does not stop the network), internet, timeout_per_script, total_timeout, python_local (the Python run outside Docker and its version), and docker: runs (for each kind of run, r_run, r_install, python_run, python_install, the image and the docker run arguments, such as --network none, --read-only, --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, the process limit and the memory and processor limits) and images (for each image, its ID and digests from docker image inspect, its creation time and the R and Python versions its environment declares).

run_results$checked says what the run of each script shows about the code, in five groups, so that a script that does not reproduce is kept apart from one the check could not test: ran (it ran to the end); code_error (it did not reproduce: it stopped with an error of the code or the deposit, could not be read, or needs a file the deposit does not hold); dependency (a package or program was not available: a package that could not be installed or was not loaded, a program outside R and Python, a system library, or R crashing in a package’s compiled code); time (it did not finish within the time limit for one script, or was not started because the time for all scripts had run out); and not_checkable (it could not be checked automatically: it needs a person, the internet, a key or another setting of the authors’ computer, one platform such as Google Colab, Windows or OpenSAFELY, more memory than the run allows, a file that was not downloaded, a screen, or a program that runs it, or it is a file of a package of the code that Python runs only as a module of that package). It is NA for files run inside another script, files that are not an analysis, files not read, and a Docker failure. summary_table counts each group (repro_ran_n, repro_code_error_n, repro_dependency_n, repro_time_n, repro_not_checkable_n), and the report’s first sentence gives them. The traffic light reflects the static readiness signals by default; a script in code_error that stopped with an error makes it red, as a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure, and a script in one of the other three groups keeps it from being green. Calls that need a screen, which the run does not have (dev.print(), dev.copy2pdf(), dev.copy2eps(), savePlot(), windows(), win.graph(), x11(), quartz(), View()), are replaced before the run by calls that need none, which modifications records as screen_call_replaced. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

This study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/8env4) and was approved by the Boston College Institutional Review Board (Protocol 25.089). All data (raw and processed), materials, analysis scripts and code, and the source of this manuscript are available at https://github.com/jgeller112/Prequestions_EyeTracking. The author has no conflicts of interest to disclose. I thank Shana Carpenter for help with the materials and with conceptualizing the study.

I Remember That Question: Using Eye Tracking to See How Prequestions Shape Reading

A common study strategy involves retrieving information from memory by answering questions after a learning event (Hartwig & Dunlosky, 2012). This technique, known as retrieval practice, has been shown to improve long-term retention across a wide range of materials and learning contexts, a phenomenon known as the testing effect (S. K. Carpenter, 2012; Dunlosky et al., 2013; Kornell & Vaughn, 2016; Roediger & Karpicke, 2006; Rowland, 2014). Surprisingly, answering questions before a learning event can also improve subsequent memory, even when learners have little prior knowledge of the material and most of their initial answers are incorrect. This phenomenon, known as the prequestion effect, is particularly intriguing because, unlike traditional retrieval practice, it does not require learners to retrieve previously studied information. Although this finding is consistent with the broader literature suggesting that effortful and even error-prone learning experiences can benefit long-term retention (Bjork, 1994), why prequestions improve learning remains unclear.

The benefits of prequestions are typically demonstrated in experiments in which learners are assigned to a prequestion group or a control group (S. K. Carpenter et al., 2023). Before encountering the learning material, the prequestion group attempts to answer questions about the upcoming content, often guessing when they do not know the answers, whereas the control group encounters the material without answering any questions. After learning, both groups complete a final memory test assessing information that was targeted by the prequestions as well as information that was not. The typical finding is that learners who received prequestions remember the targeted information better than those who did not, a phenomenon known as the specific benefit of prequestions (Pan & Carpenter, 2023). In some cases, prequestions also improve memory for information that was not directly targeted, known as a general benefit of prequestions. However, whereas the specific benefit is robust, the general benefit is less consistent. Two recent meta-analyses found substantial specific benefits (g = 0.54, St. Hilaire et al., 2024; g = 0.66, King-Shepard et al., 2025), but no reliable general benefit (g = 0.04, St. Hilaire et al., 2024; g = 0.01, King-Shepard et al., 2025). Nevertheless, some studies have reported general benefits depending on the learning materials (S. K. Carpenter & Toftness, 2017), the types of questions used (Bostan & Ozcelik, 2026; St. Hilaire et al., 2019), and the placement of non-prequestioned information relative to prequestioned content (Sana & Carpenter, 2023).

The specific benefit, by contrast, has been demonstrated acorss a wide variety of study materials and settings (S. K. Carpenter et al., 2018; S. K. Carpenter & Toftness, 2017; Geller et al., 2017; Richland et al., 2009; Soderstrom & Bjork, 2023; St. Hilaire & Carpenter, 2020; see Pan & Carpenter, 2023 for a review).

Why do preqeustions improve learning? Several non-mutually exclusive mechanisms have been proposed (King-Shepard et al., 2025; Pan & Carpenter, 2023). Prequestions may stimulate curiosity about the answers (Berlyne, 1954 (Berlyne, , 1962)), encourage elaboration by activating related prior knowledge (Kornell et al., 2009), or provide a metacognitive "reality check" that makes learners aware of gaps in their knowledge (Bjork et al., 2013). Although these explanations differ, they share the possibility that prequestions direct learners' attention toward information relevant to the questions (King-Shepard et al., 2025). According to an attentionbased account, prequestions signal which information is important, encouraging learners to attend to and process that information more thoroughly when they encounter it (Pan & Carpenter, 2023). Consistent with this account, researchers looking at eye movements during a learning episode have found that learners spend more time looking at (Bostan & Ozcelik, 2026; Yang et al., 2021), re-inspecting, and returning to prequestioned information after reading subsequent material (Lewis & Mensink, 2012).

Although these findings support an attention-based account, several results suggest that directing attention toward prequestioned information may not, by itself, fully explain the benefits of prequestions. If prequestions primarily function by signaling which information deserves attention, other methods of highlighting that information might be expected to produce similar benefits. However, answering prequestions has been found to improve memory more than studying material with the tested concepts emphasized or reading questions without answering them (Richland et al., 2009), and more than reading learning objectives or statements of the target facts (Sana et al., 2020; but see Rivers et al., 2026). Moreover, although prequestions reliably improve memory for targeted information (King-Shepard et al., 2025; St. Hilaire et al., 2024), some studies also find benefits for information that was not prequestioned (Bostan & Ozcelik, 2026; Rivers et al., 2026; Sana & Carpenter, 2023; St. Hilaire et al., 2019). Any account of the prequestion effect must therefore consider why learning benefits are sometimes restricted to prequestioned information and sometimes extend to other material.

One account that may be able to explain these differences is the attentional-window account (Sana & Carpenter, 2023). According to this account, prequestions initiate a period of heightened attention as learners search for the answers, with attention returning to baseline once the relevant information has been encountered. Information presented while this attentional window remains open may also benefit, even if it was not directly targeted by a prequestion.

Thus, whether prequestions produce a general benefit should depend partly on where the prequestioned information appears in the learning material. Supporting this prediction, Sana and Carpenter (2023) found that prequestions produced only a specific benefit when the targeted information appeared near the beginning of a passage. However, when the targeted information appeared near the end, prequestions also improved memory for non-prequestioned information encountered while learners were presumably still searching for the answers. These findings suggest that the effects of prequestions may depend on how attention is allocated throughout the learning event. Nevertheless, much of the evidence for this account comes from subsequent memory performance rather than direct observations of processing during learning.

Eye tracking provides a way to examine these attentional predictions as learning unfolds.

During reading and visual exploration, the eyes alternate between relatively brief periods of stability, known as fixations, and rapid movements between them, known as saccades. The location and duration of fixations provide measures of overt visual attention and are sensitive to cognitive processes involved in comprehension and learning (Deng & Gao, 2023; Hyönä et al., 2003; Madsen et al., 2021; Rayner, 1998; Rayner, 2009). Because eye movements can be recorded continuously without interrupting the learning experience, eye tracking allows researchers to examine how learners visually process information as they encounter it rather than inferring processing solely from subsequent memory performance (Rayner, 1998). Importantly, eye movements can distinguish processing during an initial encounter with information from subsequent reprocessing, such as rereading a sentence or returning to an earlier part of a passage.

Eye-movement measures are also sensitive to individual differences in reading ability (Ashby et al., 2005; Perfetti, 2007), prior knowledge (McNamara & Magliano, 2009), and working memory capacity (Daneman & Carpenter, 1980). Accordingly, real-time measures such as eye tracking have been identified as an important direction for prequestion research (Pan & Carpenter, 2023).

In particular, King-Shepard et al. (2025) recommended examining how prequestions influence the time learners spend processing prequestioned and non-prequestioned information during reading.

Relatively few studies have used eye tracking to investigate how prequestions influence reading. In an early study, readers who received questions before reading spent more time rereading and carefully processing question-related information while reading unrelated material more quickly (Rothkopf & Billington, 1979). Lewis and Mensink (2012) examined the effects of prequestions in two eye-tracking experiments using passages on different topics. In Experiment 1, participants read a passage about space travel after receiving one of two sets of six prequestions or no prequestions. Readers receiving one set of prequestions spent more time re-inspecting and looking back to question-relevant sentences and subsequently recalled more of that information than readers receiving the other set. However, the second set of prequestions did not produce reliable effects on reading or memory. In Experiment 2, Lewis and Mensink (2012) used a passage describing the humanitarian efforts of the Gates Foundation, including efforts to address polio and tuberculosis (TB). One group received four prequestions about TB before reading, whereas a control group read the passage without prequestions. Eye movements were recorded using a head-mounted eye tracker. Prequestions did not increase forward reading times for sentences containing the answers. Instead, readers who received prequestions spent more time rereading the targeted sentences before moving forward and made more look-backs to those sentences after proceeding to later portions of the passage. They also showed a smaller increase in look-backs to other parts of the text. On a subsequent free-recall test, the prequestion group recalled approximately twice as much of the targeted information as the control group, but did not recall more of the non-prequestioned information. Thus, the specific memory benefit was accompanied by greater reprocessing of the targeted sentences rather than slower initial reading. This pattern suggests that readers may first recognize information as relevant to a prequestion and subsequently return to process it more extensively.

More recently, Bostan and Ozcelik (2026) examined the effects of integrative prequestions, which require learners to combine information from different parts of a text.

Twelve participants received integrative prequestions before reading a passage about car brakes, whereas another twelve read the passage without prequestions. Compared with the control group, readers who received prequestions made more fixations, spent more time on targeted sentences, and made more transitions between them. Unlike most prequestion studies, the authors also observed a general benefit: participants who received prequestions performed better on questions assessing non-prequestioned information despite spending less time fixating those sentences.

These findings suggest that prequestions can alter the distribution of visual processing across a passage, although increased fixation time on particular information does not necessarily correspond to greater memory for that information.

Taken together, previous eye-tracking studies indicate that prequestions influence how learners allocate visual attention during reading (Bostan & Ozcelik, 2026; Lewis & Mensink, 2012; Yang et al., 2021). However, whether these changes contribute directly to improved memory or reflect other processes initiated by prequestions remains uncertain. Furthermore, some findings suggest that the benefits of prequestions cannot be explained simply by the amount of time learners spend processing the material. For example, in a large multisite classroom study, prequestions improved learning even though students subsequently watched less of the instructional videos, with some students skipping the videos entirely (Motz et al., 2026).

Similarly, Bostan and Ozcelik (2026) found improved memory for non-prequestioned information despite shorter fixation times on that information. Such findings suggest that prequestions may influence not only the allocation of attention but also how information is processed once encountered. One alternative explanation is the mental model hypothesis proposed by Motz et al. (2026). According to this account, prequestions activate relevant prior knowledge before learning, facilitating the processing and encoding of related information when it is subsequently encountered. As learners recognize connections between the new information and their activated knowledge, they may allocate additional attention to that content. From this perspective, increased attention may follow the recognition of relevant information rather than being the primary mechanism responsible for improved learning. Consistent with this possibility, Motz et al. (2026) found that the benefit of prequestions was greater among students who answered more prequestions correctly, suggesting that access to relevant prior knowledge may contribute to the effect. Although the attention-based and mental model accounts are not necessarily mutually exclusive, they raise an important question about the timing and nature of the processing changes associated with prequestions. In particular, determining whether prequestions influence reading when relevant information is first encountered or primarily during subsequent reprocessing may help clarify how prequestions shape learning.

The Current Study

The existing literature provides evidence that prequestions influence both memory and the allocation of visual attention during learning. However, questions remain about when these changes in visual processing emerge, whether they are specific to prequestioned information, and how prequestions alter the distribution of reading times. The current study addressed these questions by combining a counterbalanced prequestion design with eye-tracking measures that distinguish initial reading from subsequent reprocessing. We also used distributional analyses to examine how prequestions influence reading times beyond differences in average duration.

Our study builds on two previous eye-tracking investigations of prequestions during reading (Bostan & Ozcelik, 2026; Lewis & Mensink, 2012) while addressing several methodological limitations. First, in Experiment 2 of Lewis and Mensink (2012) and in Bostan and Ozcelik (2026), the same set of sentences was prequestioned for all participants in the prequestion condition. Consequently, the effects of prequestions could not be fully separated from characteristics of the particular sentences being targeted. Although Experiment 1 of Lewis and Mensink (2012) included two sets of prequestions, these targeted different numbers of sentences, and only one set reliably affected reading. In the current study, prequestioned content was fully counterbalanced so that the same sentences were read both with and without prequestions across participants.

Second, previous studies used relatively small samples, with approximately 20 participants per group in Lewis and Mensink (2012) and 12 participants per group in Bostan and Ozcelik (2026), limiting the precision of the estimated effects. In addition, Bostan and Ozcelik (2026) compared total fixation durations and counts between groups without accounting for participant-level differences in reading behavior. The current study included a substantially larger sample (138 participants, approximately 46 per condition) and used models that accounted for variation across participants and items, including sentences and test questions where appropriate.

Third, whereas previous studies primarily analyzed average reading or fixation times, we also examined the distribution of reading times to determine whether prequestions produce broader shifts in reading duration or disproportionately influence unusually long readings.

Fourth, in Lewis and Mensink (2012), participants were presented with questions and instructed to read the passage to answer them, but were not required to provide answers before reading. Although learners may have generated answers covertly, which can be as effective as overtly answering prequestions (Rivers et al., 2026), whether they did so is unknown. In the current study, participants explicitly answered each prequestion before reading, consistent with the procedure used in many prequestion studies. Finally, unlike the integrative questions used by Bostan and Ozcelik (2026), each prequestion in the current study targeted information contained within a single sentence, as in Lewis and Mensink (2012). Such questions have generally been associated with specific rather than general memory benefits (St. Hilaire et al., 2019).

In out study, participants read the Gates Foundation passage used in Experiment 2 of Lewis and Mensink (2012), which describes efforts to eradicate polio and TB. Before reading, participants answered five prequestions about polio, five prequestions about TB, or no prequestions. The passage contained ten target sentences, each providing the answer to one prequestion. By counterbalancing which topic was prequestioned, every target sentence served as prequestioned information for one group and non-prequestioned information for another. This design allowed us to compare processing of the same sentences across prequestion and noprequestion conditions while minimizing confounding between prequestion status and sentence content.

We examined two categories of eye-movement measures. Global measures, including total gaze duration, rereading time, and regressions-in (look-backs), captured processing across encounters with a sentence, including subsequent returns to it. Our local measure, selective regression-path duration, captured processing associated with the initial encounter with a sentence, before the reader progressed to later text. Distinguishing these measures allowed us to assess whether prequestions influence processing when relevant information is first encountered, during subsequent rereading, or both.

In addition to examining these measures, we used distributional analyses to characterize how prequestions influence reading times. Reading and fixation durations are typically rightskewed, with a lower bound of zero and a relatively long tail of unusually long observations (Balota & Yap, 2011; Staub et al., 2010). Consequently, statistical models that assume normally distributed reading times may not adequately characterize the observed data, and transformations intended to reduce skewness can alter the scale on which effects are evaluated (Lo & Andrews, 2015). We therefore modeled total gaze duration using the ex-Gaussian distribution, which represents response times as the sum of a Gaussian component, characterized by its mean (μ), and an exponential component, characterized by its mean (τ).

An advantage of the ex-Gaussian distribution is that it allows changes in the location of the Gaussian component to be distinguished from changes in the exponential component contributing to the right tail. Although these parameters are descriptive and do not uniquely identify underlying cognitive processes (Matzke & Wagenmakers, 2009), previous research suggests that experimental manipulations can influence them differently. For example, word frequency has been found to affect both μ and τ in fixation durations during reading (Staub et al., 2010), whereas modest visual degradation of text primarily affected μ (White & Staub, 2012).

Similarly, in scene viewing, image type influenced μ, whereas familiarity increased τ, reflecting a greater contribution from longer fixations (Guy et al., 2020). These findings illustrate how experimental manipulations may alter different characteristics of the reading-time distribution. This distinction may be particularly informative for understanding prequestion effects. If prequestions lead readers to recognize particular sentences as relevant and sometimes engage in additional processing or reanalysis, they may disproportionately increase longer reading times rather than uniformly slowing reading. Analyses of average reading duration alone cannot distinguish these possibilities. We therefore examined both ex-Gaussian parameters. An effect on μ would indicate a shift in the Gaussian component of the reading-time distribution, whereas an effect on τ would indicate a greater contribution from the exponential component and its right tail. Although neither pattern provides a unique signature of a cognitive mechanism, these analyses allow a more detailed characterization of how prequestions change reading behavior.

Hypotheses

For final test performance, we predicted a specific benefit of prequestions: participants would remember more information about the prequestioned topic than participants in the noprequestion condition. Based on prior findings that general benefits are less consistent, particularly for questions targeting individual pieces of information (King-Shepard et al., 2025; St. Hilaire et al., 2019), we did not predict a general benefit for the non-prequestioned topic. We compared performance for prequestioned and non-prequestioned information against performance for the same material in the no-prequestion condition, both overall and separately for each topic.

For eye movements, we predicted that prequestioned sentences would receive longer total gaze durations and more rereading than the same sentences encountered without prequestions.

Specifically, we expected an interaction between prequestion condition and topic, such that Polio prequestions would selectively increase processing of polio-related sentences, whereas TB prequestions would selectively increase processing of TB-related sentences. We also examined whether these changes emerged during initial reading or subsequent reprocessing. Finally, our distributional analyses assessed whether differences in total gaze duration were associated with changes in the Gaussian component (μ), the exponential component (τ), or both.

Method

We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures included in the study. The study was preregistered (https://osf.io/8env4). All data, materials, and analysis scripts are available at https://github.com/jgeller112/Prequestions_EyeTracking. All reported statistics, tables, and figures were generated from the raw data using the code in that repository. Generative AI (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) was used to assist with editing the manuscript and code as well as help organzie all the data and code on the repository.

The author verified the content and citations and takes full responsibility for the manuscript.

Participants

The target sample size was determined based on the specific benefit of prequestions. A recent meta-analysis reported a medium-sized effect (g = 0. 54; St. Hilaire et al. (2024)), which we converted to an odds ratio of 2.66 for the preregistered binomial mixed-effects model. A simulation-based power analysis using mixedpower (Kumle et al., 2021), informed by pilot data, indicated that 45 participants per condition would provide 90% power to detect an effect of this magnitude. We therefore planned to recruit 135 participants, with 45 assigned to each of the three conditions.

Participants were recruited from the Boston College SONA participant pool and received course credit. Eye-tracking data were recorded from 161 participants. One participant had eyetracking data for fewer than all four pages of the text and was excluded. Eighteen participants did not meet the preregistered calibration criterion (accuracy and precision of 0.5° or better) or could not be calibrated and were excluded. Four participants had no final test data and were excluded.

The final sample comprised 138 participants (no prequestions: 47; Polio prequestions: 45; TB prequestions: 46). Calibration validation data were available for all included participants. Mean calibration accuracy was 0.37° (SD = 0.10, range 0.13-0.50), and mean precision, defined as the standard deviation of gaze samples, was 0.22° (SD = 0.12, range 0.06-0.49). All included participants with available calibration data met the preregistered criterion of 0.5° or better for both accuracy and precision. Before reading, participants rated their familiarity with polio and tuberculosis on a scale from 0 (never heard of it) to 100 (expert). Familiarity was low (polio: M = 24.1, SD = 16.8; tuberculosis: M = 29.4, SD = 18.8; ratings were available for 109 of the 138 participantsfoot_0 ) and similar across conditions, so the preregistered exclusion based on prior knowledge, for which no criterion had been specified, was not applied.

Materials

Participants read a 690-word passage used by Lewis and Mensink (2012) describing the Gates Foundation's humanitarian efforts to eradicate polio and tuberculosis (TB) in developing countries. The passage contained 38 sentences presented across four pages, each consisting of 16-17 lines (Figure 1). Ten sentences served as targets: five concerning polio (M = 19.4 words, SD = 11.4, range 4-35) and five concerning TB (M = 16.2 words, SD = 3.7, range 11-21).

The polio target sentences had a higher reading level than the TB target sentences, as assessed by the Flesch-Kincaid grade level (Kincaid et al., 1975), calculated using the quanteda package (Benoit et al., 2018) (polio: M = 14.1, SD = 6.2; TB: M = 8.8, SD = 2.0). However, the two sets of sentences were similar in syntactic complexity, estimated using dependency parsing with UDPipe (Straka & Straková, 2017; Wijffels & Straka, 2026) and its English Web Treebank model (Silveira et al., 2014). We examined mean dependency distance (Liu, 2008), defined as the average number of words separating a word from its syntactic head (polio: M = 2.72, SD = 1.03; TB: M = 2.62, SD = 0.40), and the number of clauses per sentence (polio: M = 1.6, SD = 0.9; TB: M = 1.8, SD = 0.8).

Each target sentence contained the answer to one of ten short-answer questions (five about polio and five about TB; Appendix A). Questions required percentage-based, yes/no, or multipart responses. The maximum possible score was 12 points per topic and 24 points overall.

The study included three conditions: polio prequestions, TB prequestions, and no prequestions. Participants in the polio and TB conditions answered five questions about their assigned topic before reading, whereas participants in the no-prequestion condition read the passage without answering questions beforehand. For each prequestion condition, the five target sentences corresponding to the assigned topic were classified as prequestioned, and the five sentences about the other topic were classified as non-prequestioned. Thus, across conditions, every target sentence served as both prequestioned and non-prequestioned information, allowing the effects of prequestions to be separated from differences in sentence content.

Apparatus

Eye movements were recorded using a Tobii Pro Spectrum eye tracker sampling at 600 Hz. The passage was displayed on a 23.8-inch EIZO FlexScan EV2451 monitor (1920 × 1080 pixels) viewed from approximately 65 cm without a chin rest. Text was presented in 36-point Courier New, a monospaced font, against a grey background. At this viewing distance, each character subtended approximately 0.5° of visual angle, and the line spacing subtended approximately 1.1°.

The experiment was administered using Tobii Pro Lab (version 25.19). The prequestions, distractor task, and final test were programmed in PsychoPy, hosted on Pavlovia, and embedded as web elements within the Tobii Pro Lab timeline.

Procedure

At the beginning of the session, participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: polio prequestions, TB prequestions, or no prequestions. The experiment consisted of four phases: prequestions, reading, a distractor task, and a final test. Participants in the noprequestion condition skipped the prequestion phase.

Prequestions

Participants in the two prequestion conditions answered five short-answer questions about their assigned topic (polio or TB), presented in random order (https://run.pavlovia.org/Jgeller 112/preq). They were informed that they might not know the correct answers and were encouraged to provide their best guesses. Each question appeared individually on the screen, with a text box below it for entering a response. Participants had unlimited time to respond and clicked a triangle at the bottom of the screen to advance to the next question. No feedback was provided.

Reading

Before reading, participants completed Tobii Pro Lab's nine-point calibration procedure, which presented white targets against a grey background. Calibration accuracy and precision were then validated and recorded. Participants subsequently read the four-page passage while their eye movements were recorded. They advanced through the pages at their own pace, with no time limit, but could not return to previously viewed pages.

Distractor Task

After reading, all participants completed a president recognition task (https://run. pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preq_president) that served as a distractor and lasted approximately 3 minutes.

Final Test

Participants completed a final test consisting of all ten short-answer questions (five about polio and five about TB), presented in random order (https://run.pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preQ_test). The response format was identical to that used during the prequestion phase, with unlimited response time and no feedback. For participants in the prequestion conditions, five questions were repeated from the prequestion phase, whereas the remaining five were new. Participants were then thanked and debriefed.

Scoring

Prequestion and final-test responses were scored using a deterministic, rule-based scoring procedure developed with the assistance of Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic; model ID claudeopus-5-5). Rather than scoring individual responses directly, Claude generated an R scoring script (scoring_rubric.R, used by grade_prequestions.R and grade_test.R) that applied the same predefined criteria to all responses. The script awarded one point for each required element of a correct answer present in a participant's response. Question-specific scoring criteria are provided in Appendix A.

To assess scoring reliability, a research assistant who was blind to experimental condition, test phase, and automated scores independently scored all 1,678 nonblank responses.

The automated and human scores agreed exactly on 97.6% of responses. Agreement was excellent, ICC(2,1) = .99, 95% CI [.99, .99], based on a two-way random-effects, absoluteagreement, single-measure intraclass correlation coefficient (Koo & Li, 2016; Shrout & Fleiss, 1979), calculated using the irr package (Gamer et al., 2026). Agreement for participants' total final-test scores was also excellent, ICC(2,1) = .99. Question-level agreement statistics are reported in Table A2. All analyses used the automated scores.

Eye-Movement Data Processing

Sentence-level measures were computed from the fixation-level data. Fixations were identified with Tobii Pro Lab's Tobii I-VT (Fixation) filter, a velocity-threshold identification algorithm (Olsen, 2012; Salvucci & Goldberg, 2000), with the following settings. Gaps in the gaze data shorter than 75 ms (e.g., brief losses of tracking) were filled by linear interpolation, the gaze positions of the two eyes were averaged, and noise was reduced with a moving median over a window of three samples. A gaze sample was classified as part of a fixation when the angular velocity of the eye, computed over a 20-ms window, was below 30°/s. Adjacent fixations separated by less than 75 ms and less than 0.5° of visual angle were merged, and fixations shorter than 60 ms were discarded. Fixations cut off when a page appeared or disappeared can nonetheless be shorter than 60 ms in the export. We excluded fixations shorter than 80 ms (4.0% of fixations) and longer than 1,000 ms (0.06%) before any further processing. Both bounds follow common practice in reading research: 80 ms is the most common lower bound, and 800, 1,000, and 1,200 ms are the most common upper bounds (Schotter & Dillon, 2025; e.g., Serrano-Carot et al., 2025). Very short fixations are unlikely to reflect processing of the text and include fixations cut short by a page change. Most fixations in reading last around 200 ms (Rayner, 1998; Schotter & Dillon, 2025); in the present data the median fixation lasted 178 ms, so a single fixation longer than 1,000 ms, 5.6 times the median, is unlikely to reflect ongoing reading and more likely reflects a lapse of attention or a brief loss of the eye-tracking signal that the fixation filter bridged.

The remaining processing (derive_et_measures.R) proceeded in four steps. (a) The exact layout of each page was reconstructed from the sentence texts and full-resolution screenshots of the pages (monospaced font, 79 characters per line), giving the screen position of every character of every sentence (Figure 1). (b) Each fixation was assigned to a text line after correcting for vertical drift, separately for each reader and page, with a procedure that combines two approaches used in automated drift-correction algorithms (Carr et al., 2022): assigning sequences of fixations to a line together, and modelling drift as a function of position on the page (details in Appendix D). The correction was limited to the calibration accuracy criterion of 0.5° (0.57 cm, about 0.45 of a line spacing), so it could not move a reader's gaze by a whole line. (c) Each fixation was then assigned to the sentence occupying its line and horizontal position: its character column was computed from the fixed character width, a fixation on a space took the sentence of the nearest letter, and fixations more than three characters beyond either end of a line were treated as off the text. (d) Reading on each page was taken to start at the first fixation on the page's first sentence; fixations before that (the landing) contributed to total time but not to firstpass measures. After processing, 96.8% of on-screen fixations were assigned to a sentence, and the assigned sentence agreed with Tobii Pro Lab's assignment for 89.8% of fixations. First-pass reading was identified for 96.9% of fixated target sentences. Figure 2 shows one reader's fixations on one page before and after processing. For this reader, the correction moved fixations by a median of 0.44 line spacings and changed the sentence assigned to 43.4% of fixations; the medians over all readers and pages were 0.24 line spacings and 8.2%. The Four Text Pages and the Sentence Regions Used as Areas of Interest Note. Each sentence is one area of interest, made of one rectangle per text line it occupies. Polio target sentences are shown in blue, TB target sentences in vermillion (orange-red), and other sentences in grey; numbers give each sentence's position on its page. Eye-Movement Measures

All measures were computed for each participant and target sentence. Durations were divided by the number of words in the sentence (ms per word), because target sentences differed in length. Only sentences that were fixated were analysed: a target sentence that received no fixation has no reading time, so its measures were treated as missing (17 of 1380 target sentences, 1.2%). Following the eye-movement literature, we distinguish global measures, which reflect all processing of a sentence including later returns to it, from local measures, which reflect processing when the sentence is first encountered (Figure 3). Eye-Movement Measures, Illustrated With a Schematic Reading Example Note. Definitions follow Schotter and Dillon (2025). The circles are fixations, numbered in time order (arrows: saccades; dashed arrows: regressions; dotted arrows: moves to the next line); the shaded sentence is the target, and each fixation is coloured by the measure it counts towards for the target. Selective regression-path duration (first-pass reading; also called right-bounded reading time or selective go-past time) sums the fixations on the sentence from first entering it until the eyes first move past it to later text; fixations on earlier text during this period (here, 6) are not counted and do not end it. Total gaze duration sums all fixations on the sentence.

Regression-in records whether the eyes returned to the sentence from later text (0/1). Re-reading time sums the fixations on the sentence after the reader had first moved on to later text (operationalizing the preregistered "re-reading durations back to the prequestioned information"). Selective regression-path duration is defined only for sentences fixated before any later sentence (not skipped). The duration measures do not overlap: total gaze duration is the sum of selective regression-path duration, re-reading time, and any fixations made before reading started on the page. Global measures include later returns to the sentence; the local measure reflects processing when the sentence is first encountered. The preregistered first-pass duration (fixations until the sentence is first exited) would here be 3 + 4 + 5 only, cut short by the brief return at 6; it was replaced by selective regression-path duration (see Statistical Analysis). All durations were divided by the number of words in the sentence (ms per word).

Statistical Analysis

All analyses were conducted in R version 4.6.1 (R Core Team, 2026). 2 The effects of prequestions on test performance and eye movements were estimated with Bayesian mixed models in brms (Bürkner, 2017), which fits models in Stan (B. Carpenter et al., 2017), run through cmdstanr (Gabry et al., 2025) with CmdStan 2.37.0. Each target sentence, and each finaltest question, was coded by its status for the reader: prequestioned (Polio sentences and questions for readers in the Polio condition, TB sentences and questions for readers in the TB condition), non-prequestioned (the other topic for those readers), or no-prequestion (both topics for readers in the no-prequestion condition). The main models pooled the two prequestion conditions, with Status and Topic (Polio, TB) as fixed effects. The specific effect of prequestions was the difference prequestioned -no-prequestion: the same sentences or questions for readers whose prequestions they answered and for readers who saw no prequestions. The general effect was non-prequestioned -no-prequestion. Because each topic contributes equally to the prequestioned, non-prequestioned, and no-prequestion cells, differences between the Polio and TB materials cancel in these comparisons. Both the specific and general effects and their breakdown by topic were preregistered. To break the effects down by topic, we fitted the preregistered Group (Polio prequestions, TB prequestions, or no prequestions) × Topic (Polio, TB) models with the same families and priors. Following the preregistered hypotheses, we estimated the Polio -TB difference within each group-predicted to be positive in the Polio group, negative in the TB group, and absent in the no-prequestion group-and the Group × Topic interaction contrast, the Polio group's Polio -TB difference minus the TB group's, predicted to be positive. Because the Polio and TB sentences (and questions) are different items, each withingroup Polio -TB difference combines any effect of prequestions with differences between the items, and with five items per topic, the population-level topic difference is estimated imprecisely. Each within-group difference was therefore interpreted together with the interaction contrast, in which the item differences cancel because both groups read the same items.

Reading times are strongly right-skewed, so no duration was analysed with a Gaussian model. As preregistered for heavily skewed durations, total gaze duration was analysed with an ex-Gaussian distributional model ({cogmod}; Makowski (2026)), which describes a duration as the sum of a Gaussian component, whose mean μ reflects typical reading time, and an exponential component, whose mean τ reflects the tail of unusually long readings. The mean of an ex-Gaussian distribution is μ + τ and its standard deviation is √(σ² + τ²), where σ is the standard deviation of the Gaussian component, so μ and τ are components of reading time rather than reading times themselves. The fixed and random effects applied to both μ and τ, and σ had by-participant random intercepts. The preregistered first-pass duration, from first entering a sentence until first leaving it, could not be described by any of the distributions we considered (ex-Gaussian, Gamma, lognormal), because it mixes two kinds of first pass. About half of first passes, in all three conditions, were cut short after a few fixations by a brief return to the preceding line, so the distribution had two modes: interrupted first passes of a few hundred milliseconds and complete first readings of several seconds. First-pass reading was therefore measured as selective regression-path duration [also called right-bounded reading time; Schotter and Dillon (2025)]: the time spent on the sentence from first entering it until the eyes first moved past it to later text, so that brief returns to earlier text did not end it and time spent on earlier text was not counted (Figure 3). Its distribution was unimodal and right-skewed and closely described by the ex-Gaussian, so it was analysed with the same ex-Gaussian model as total gaze duration (μ and τ). Re-reading time was the time spent on a sentence after the reader had first moved on to later text, so that the two measures do not overlap (cf. rereading time in Schotter & Dillon, 2025). Whether readers returned to a sentence from later text is captured by regressions-in (0/1), which were analysed with logistic models; re-reading time was analysed for the 37.5% of sentences that were re-read, with a Gamma model with a log link, which models positive, rightskewed durations without transforming them (Lo & Andrews, 2015); the ex-Gaussian was not suitable, because re-reading times were close to exponentially distributed, so that its Gaussian component collapsed (σ near zero). The model therefore describes how long readers re-read a sentence once they had returned to it. Because the questions were worth different numbers of points (1-4), final test performance was analysed as the points earned on each question out of its maximum, with a beta-binomial model: a binomial model of the points earned with an additional parameter for overdispersion, because a participant tends to know all or none of a question's elements. Effects are reported on the scale of the expected proportion of a question's points, which puts all questions on the same 0-1 scale. Because each question has at most four points, scores can take only a few values (0, .25, .33, .50, .67, .75, and 1). In posterior predictive checks, the beta-binomial model reproduced how often each score occurred (predicted and observed shares within 1.1 percentage points), better than a binomial model without overdispersion.

Prequestion performance was analysed in the same way, comparing the two prequestion conditions.

All models included the maximal random-effects structure warranted by the design (Barr et al., 2013). Topic varied within participants, so the models included by-participant random intercepts and Topic slopes (the preregistered structure). Every target sentence and every finaltest question was prequestioned for one group, non-prequestioned for another, and read or answered by the no-prequestion group, so Status (and Group) varied within items, and the models also included by-sentence (eye movements) or by-question (final test) random intercepts and Status (or Group) slopes. Within a participant, Status is determined by Topic, so no byparticipant Status slope was possible. In the prequestion model, condition varied between participants and between questions, so it included random intercepts for participants and questions only. Status, Condition, and Topic were coded with equal-prior contrasts [contr.equalprior_pairs; {bayestestR}, Makowski, Ben-Shachar, and Lüdecke (2019)]. With this coding, a normal(0, s) prior on the coefficients implies the same normal(0, s) prior on every pairwise difference between conditions, so that no condition serves as a reference with a different prior, and every comparison is tested against the same prior. s was set on each model's link scale: 1.5 on the log-odds scale (regressions-in, final test, and prequestions; an odds ratio of 4.5 for one SD), 0.5 on the log scale of the Gamma models and on the scale of τ (a factor of about 1.65 for one SD), and 100 ms per word for μ.

Intercepts, random-effect standard deviations, and correlations had weakly informative priors (Appendix B). Each model was sampled with four chains of 10000 post-warm-up iterations (40000 posterior draws, enough for stable Bayes factors). All models converged: there were no divergent transitions, all R-hat values were below 1.001, and all bulk effective sample sizes exceeded 4900.

Means and comparisons were computed on the response scale by averaging each posterior draw's predictions over the observed sample (modelbased with the {marginaleffects} (Arel-Bundock et al., 2024) backend and estimate = "average"), so that they incorporate the variation due to the random effects. Durations are reported in ms per word, and probabilities and proportions in percent. Effects were summarized by their posterior mean, credible interval (CrI), and probability of direction (pd), the proportion of the posterior with the same sign as its median.

The pd is closely related to the frequentist p value: for a one-tailed test, p ≈ 1 -pd, and for a twotailed test, p ≈ 2(1 -pd), so pd > 95% corresponds to a one-tailed p < .05 (Makowski, Ben-Shachar, Chen, et al., 2019). The predictions for the specific effects and for prequestioned versus non-prequestioned material were directional (longer reading, more regressions, better recall), so we treated such an effect as present when pd > 95% in the predicted direction and report it with a 90% CrI, the interval that corresponds to a one-sided test at α = .05. The general effects had no directional prediction, so for them we required pd > 97.5%, corresponding to a two-tailed p < .05, and report a 95% CrI. Comparisons that were described but not tested are also reported with a 95% CrI. Bayes factors were not used as a decision criterion; we report them to describe the strength of the evidence for or against each effect. Because pd only indicates the direction of an effect and cannot provide evidence that an effect is absent, we also computed Bayes factors.

Each Bayes factor compares a model in which the comparison equals 0 with one in which it is free, using the Savage-Dickey density ratio (Wagenmakers et al., 2010): the posterior density of the comparison at 0 divided by its prior density at 0. The prior densities came from the same models sampled from their priors only, and both densities were computed for the comparisons on the link scale, where the equal priors apply. For τ and for the expected re-reading time, which have no single link scale, they were computed on the response scale; for the expected re-reading time, at the population level (without random effects), because averaging over random effects drawn from their priors produced prior draws too extreme for a density estimate. For the Group × Topic comparisons of look-backs and final test scores, the Bayes factors were also computed on the response scale (probabilities and proportions of points), the scale of the estimates. These comparisons involve different Polio and TB items, some of which had outcomes near 0 or 1, and for such outcomes the same comparison is much less precise in log-odds than in probability, so link-scale Bayes factors could contradict the estimates. BF10 > 3 indicates moderate, BF10 > 10 strong, BF10 > 30 very strong, and BF10 > 100 extreme evidence for a difference, and BF01 = 1/BF10 the corresponding evidence for no difference; values between 1/3 and 3 are anecdotal (Lee & Wagenmakers, 2014). Because a Bayes factor depends on the prior, all comparisons between conditions received the same prior, and we report how sensitive the posteriors were to the priors [power-scaling sensitivity; Kallioinen et al. (2023)].

Deviations From the Preregistration

Deviations from the preregistration, the reasons for them, and their likely effect on the results are listed in Appendix C (Table C1).

Results

Prequestion Performance

As intended, participants knew little of the material before reading. Participants in the Polio prequestion condition earned 4.1% of the available points on the prequestions (SD = 5.2%) and those in the TB prequestion condition 10.5% (SD = 10.9%). Participants attempted 43.1% (Polio) and 39.6% (TB) of the prequestions; the rest were left blank or answered "I don't know".

In a beta-binomial model of the points earned on each prequestion, with random intercepts for participants and questions, prequestion scores were similar in the two conditions (modelestimated scores: 10.6% in the TB and 8.6% in the Polio condition), TB -Polio: 2.0 percentage points, 95% CrI [-2.0, 6.0], pd = 83.0%.

Final Test Performance

Final test performance was analysed as the proportion of each question's points earned (Figure 4). Pooled over the two prequestion conditions, participants earned 62.2% of the points on their prequestioned topic, compared with 45.6% for no-prequestion participants on the same questions, a specific benefit of 16.7 percentage points, 90% CrI [13.2, 20.1], pd > 99.9%, BF10 = 1.3 × 10 8 : extreme evidence for a difference. On the non-prequestioned topic they earned 41.0%, numerically slightly lower than in the no-prequestion condition, -4.6 percentage points, 95% CrI [-8.9, -0.3], pd = 98.1%, BF01 = 1.85. There was therefore no general benefit. Although the difference met the preregistered criterion (pd > 97.5%) in the direction of a cost, the Bayes factor was inconclusive, providing only anecdotal evidence for no difference, so we do not interpret it as a general cost.

Eye Movements

Without prequestions, readers spent on average 249 ms per word on a target sentence in total (SD = 136; about 241 words per minute), 215 ms per word (SD = 109) of it in first-pass reading (selective regression-path duration). The ex-Gaussian estimates below divide such reading times into a typical part (μ) and a tail (τ), which sum to the mean. We first compare prequestioned and non-prequestioned sentences with the same sentences read by no-prequestion readers (Table 1), and then test the preregistered Group × Topic crossover (Figure 5). Figure 5 shows the posterior distributions of the means for every measure, pooled and by group.

Prequestioned and Non-Prequestioned Sentences Versus the No-Prequestion Condition

Prequestions changed how readers read the sentences that answered them, compared with no-prequestion readers reading the same sentences (Table 1). During first-pass reading, measured as selective regression-path duration, typical reading time did not differ, μ: -5.0 ms per word, 90% CrI [-17.2, 7.2], pd = 75.0%, BF01 = 12.13, with strong evidence for no difference. The tail of unusually long first-pass readings, however, was longer for prequestioned sentences, τ: 17.1 ms per word, 90% CrI [1.5, 32.8], pd = 96.4%, BF10 = 1.25, although the Bayes factor provided only anecdotal evidence for a difference. Total gaze duration showed the same pattern more clearly: prequestioned sentences had a longer tail, τ: 33.9 ms per word, 90% CrI [15.4, 52.7], pd = 99.9%, BF10 = 31.07, very strong evidence for a difference, whereas typical reading time did not differ, μ: 2.8 ms per word, 90% CrI [-9.2, 14.8], pd = 64.7%, BF01 = 14.26, with strong evidence for no difference. After moving on, readers were more likely to return to prequestioned sentences from later text (37.6% vs. 30.2%), 7.3 percentage points, 90% CrI [3.2, 11.4], pd = 99.8%, BF10 = 1.67, anecdotal evidence, and when they returned, they re-read prequestioned sentences for longer (129.2 ms per word vs. 100.0 ms per word), 29.2 ms per word, 90% CrI [11.2, 47.6], pd = 99.6%, BF10 = 9.49, moderate evidence.

Non-prequestioned sentences, by contrast, were read like the same sentences in the noprequestion condition. No measure showed a general effect (non-prequestioned -noprequestion, Table 1; all pd < 97.5%), and on every measure the Bayes factor favoured its absence (BF01 from 3.7 to 15.4), with moderate or stronger evidence on every measure. The effects of prequestions on reading were therefore specific to the prequestioned sentences.
